cultures/culture-late-antiquity/panels/0: After Chalcedon, Byzantine, Coptic, West Syriac, East Syriac, Armenian and Ethiopian rites developed distinct languages and anaphoras. In the West, Roman, Gallican, Mozarabic and Celtic uses coexisted, while Hagia Sophia's liturgy set the Byzantine standard.
cultures/culture-late-antiquity/panels/1: Romanos the Melodist composed long sung sermons (kontakia) in Constantinople. Roman chant later attributed to Gregory the Great developed, and Ethiopian tradition credits Yared with creating Ge'ez liturgical chant in the 6th century.
cultures/culture-late-antiquity/panels/2: Justinian's Hagia Sophia crowned a basilica with a vast dome; Ravenna's San Vitale and Sant'Apollinare display Byzantine mosaics. Armenia developed centralised domed stone churches, and the Ethiopian monastery of Debre Damo preserves Aksumite style.
cultures/culture-late-antiquity/panels/3: The earliest surviving icons, such as the encaustic Christ Pantocrator at Sinai, date from the 6th century. Insular manuscripts like the Lindisfarne Gospels (c. 700) and the Syriac Rabbula Gospels (586) combine text and imagery.
cultures/culture-late-antiquity/panels/4: Benedict's Rule, Irish monasteries such as Iona and Bangor, Justinian's Sinai monastery and the great East Syriac monasteries of Mount Izla shaped Christian culture. Monasteries became centres of learning, mission and economic life.
cultures/culture-late-antiquity/panels/5: Marian feasts (Annunciation, Dormition) and the Exaltation of the Cross entered the calendar, and cults of local saints flourished around relics. Disputes over computing Easter, such as at Whitby, mattered for unity.
cultures/culture-late-antiquity/panels/6: Empress Theodora protected Miaphysite clergy; Abbess Hilda of Whitby ruled a double monastery that trained five bishops. Royal women such as Bertha of Kent and Theodelinda of the Lombards influenced conversions.
cultures/culture-late-antiquity/panels/7: The School of Nisibis and Syriac scholars translated Greek philosophy and medicine, later passing it to Arabic. In the West, Boethius, Cassiodorus, Isidore of Seville and Bede preserved classical learning in monastic schools.
cultures/culture-late-antiquity/panels/8: Irish monks (Columba, Columbanus), Roman missionaries to England and Boniface in Germany spread Latin Christianity. Church of the East monks reached Central Asia and Tang China (635), Nubian kingdoms became Christian, and Thomas Christians flourished in India.
cultures/culture-late-antiquity/panels/9: The Himyarite massacre of Christians at Najran (c. 523) prompted Aksumite intervention. Under Persian and later Muslim rulers Christians faced periodic persecution, while Byzantium coerced Miaphysites and Monothelite dissidents like Maximus.
cultures/culture-late-antiquity/panels/1: Visigothic Spain enacted harsh anti-Jewish laws and forced conversions, and Heraclius ordered Jews baptised. Gregory the Great opposed forced baptism and protected synagogues, setting a papal precedent.

After 634 most Middle Eastern and North African Christians came under Muslim rule as dhimmis, paying the jizya but keeping churches. Christians served the Umayyads, and John of Damascus wrote the first Christian critique of Islam as a Christian heresy.

Justinian described church and empire as two gifts of God in harmony (symphonia), but enforced orthodoxy by law. In the West the papacy became a political force in Rome, and Frankish, Visigothic and Anglo-Saxon kings became patrons of the church.
cultures/culture-carolingian-schism/pane: Roman liturgy for the Franks; Slavonic for the East

Charlemagne imposed the Roman rite and its chant across his empire, while Cyril and Methodius introduced Slavonic liturgy. Private Masses multiplied in Western monasteries, and the Byzantine liturgy took on its classic shape with icon screens.
Gregorian chant and neumes

Frankish cantors codified 'Gregorian' chant and invented neumes to notate melody in the 9th century; early polyphony (organum) appears in treatises around 900. Byzantine hymnographers such as Theodore the Studite and Kassia wrote canons and troparia.
Cross-in-square and the first Romanesque

Middle Byzantine churches adopted the compact cross-in-square plan with a central dome over four columns, spread to Rus' and the Balkans. Carolingian Aachen chapel and, after 1000, 'First Romanesque' stone churches emerged in the West.
Icons restored; illuminated books

After iconoclasm ended (843), Byzantine churches received systematic programmes of mosaics with Christ Pantocrator in the dome. In the West the Book of Kells and Carolingian gospel books combined Insular and classical styles.
Cluny, Athos and Studios

Benedict of Aniane standardised Benedictine life; Cluny (910) led a reform focused on liturgy. The Studite monastery and Athos (963) shaped Byzantine monasticism; Church of the East monasteries existed from Baghdad to China until 845.
All Saints and the year

All Saints (1 November) spread in the West in the 9th century; the Triumph of Orthodoxy was added in Byzantium in 843. Counting years Anno Domini, popularised by Bede, spread through Carolingian usage.
Abbesses, empresses and hymnographers

Empresses Irene and Theodora restored icons; the poet-nun Kassia composed hymns still sung. Princess Olga of Kyiv was baptised c. 957, and Saxon canonesses such as Hrotsvitha wrote plays and histories.
Carolingian renaissance and Byzantine learning

Alcuin's palace school, cathedral schools and Caroline minuscule script preserved Latin texts. Photius' Bibliotheca summarised hundreds of books, and in Baghdad Christian scholars such as Hunayn ibn Ishaq translated Greek science into Arabic.
Slavs, Scandinavians and steppe peoples
Byzantine missions reached Moravia, Bulgaria and Rus'; Latin missions reached Poland, Hungary and Scandinavia. The Church of the East converted the Kerait and other Turkic peoples of Central Asia.
Vikings, Huichang and al-Hakim

Viking raids destroyed monasteries like Lindisfarne (793) and Iona. In China, the Huichang persecution (845) ended the Tang church; in Egypt and Syria the caliph al-Hakim persecuted Christians and destroyed the Holy Sepulchre (1009).
Jews in Carolingian and Byzantine society

Jewish merchants enjoyed Carolingian protection, which Agobard of Lyon protested. Byzantine emperors such as Basil I attempted forced conversions; Jewish communities in Islamic Spain and Baghdad flourished.
Living under the caliphs

Christians remained majorities in many Middle Eastern regions, serving as physicians and officials while gradually Arabising; Coptic and Syriac churches produced Arabic theology. In Spain, Mozarabic Christians lived under Córdoba, and the Córdoba martyrs (850s) protested assimilation.
Pope, emperor and basileus

Charlemagne's coronation created rival claims to Roman empire. Western rulers controlled bishoprics and monasteries (proprietary churches), while Byzantine emperors appointed patriarchs; both tensions fed the coming Gregorian reform and the schism.
cultures/culture-high-middle-ages/panels: Eucharistic devotion and the Divine Liturgy

In the West the elevation of the host and the feast of Corpus Christi (1264) focused piety on Christ's presence; lay communion was rare but annual confession was required after 1215. Orthodox worship completed its fusion of Studite and Jerusalem typika, and Ethiopian worship centred on the tabot (altar tablet).
Polyphony and troubadour piety

The Notre-Dame school (Léonin, Pérotin) developed measured polyphony; Hildegard composed vivid monophonic chant. Franciscans popularised vernacular laude, and Byzantine chant developed elaborate kalophonic styles.
Romanesque and Gothic

Pilgrimage churches such as Santiago de Compostela used massive Romanesque vaults; from 1140 Abbot Suger's Saint-Denis launched Gothic with pointed arches and stained glass, culminating in Chartres. In Ethiopia, Lalibela's churches were carved from living rock; Vladimir-Suzdal built white-stone churches.
Stained glass and icons

Gothic windows and sculpted portals taught the Bible to the unlettered. Komnenian Byzantine art brought new emotional depth (the Vladimir Mother of God), and Western painters like Cimabue began to absorb Byzantine models.
Cistercians and friars

Cistercians pursued austerity and manual labour; Carthusians solitude; military orders (Templars, Hospitallers) fused monastic vows with knighthood. Franciscans and Dominicans took religious life into the cities, while Beguines lived devout lives without vows.
Pilgrimage and jubilee
Pilgrimage to Rome, Compostela, Canterbury and Jerusalem structured devotion and economy. Feasts of Corpus Christi and the Holy Name were added, and the first Jubilee year was proclaimed in 1300.
Mystics, abbesses and beguines

Hildegard of Bingen, Clare of Assisi, Elisabeth of Hungary and the Beguines of the Low Countries pursued varied forms of holiness. Cults of the Virgin flourished, while Cathar 'perfects' included women.
Universities and scholasticism

Universities at Bologna, Paris and Oxford organised theology as a science; Peter Lombard's Sentences became the textbook. Aristotle reached the West via Arabic and Jewish scholars; Aquinas and Bonaventure synthesised faith and reason. Byzantium maintained its own higher learning.
Crusade, mendicants and the Mongols

Northern crusades forcibly Christianised the Baltic peoples. Franciscans travelled to the Mongol court and to Khanbaliq, meeting a Church of the East that had metropolitans from Baghdad to China; Rabban Sauma journeyed the other way.
Heresy and crusade
The Albigensian Crusade and the papal Inquisition targeted Cathars and Waldensians. Crusaders massacred Jews and Muslims in the Rhineland and Jerusalem, and in 1204 sacked Christian Constantinople.
Expulsions and blood libel
Crusade-era massacres, the blood libel (Norwich 1144), Lateran IV's distinctive dress and the burning of the Talmud in Paris (1242) marked a sharp deterioration. England expelled its Jews in 1290.
Crusade, convivencia and dialogue

Crusades and the Reconquista pitted Latin Christians against Muslim powers, while in Spain and Sicily translation flourished. Francis met Sultan al-Kamil; Eastern Christians under Mamluks suffered reprisals for the crusades, and the Ilkhans briefly favoured Christians before converting to Islam.
Papal monarchy

Gregory VII's reform freed episcopal elections from lay control; Innocent III claimed authority over kings. Canossa and the Concordat of Worms defined boundaries, and Byzantine emperors continued to dominate their patriarchs.
cultures/culture-late-medieval/panels/0/: Lay people heard Mass, joined confraternities and processions, and prayed with books of hours and rosaries; chantries funded Masses for the dead. Russian worship flourished with high iconostases, and Ethiopian worship was shaped by Zara Yaqob's liturgical reforms.
cultures/culture-late-medieval/panels/1/: Composers like Machaut wrote complete polyphonic Mass settings, and Dufay and Josquin developed the Renaissance Mass. Hussites sang vernacular hymns, and Russian znamenny chant developed.
cultures/culture-late-medieval/panels/2/: Late Gothic produced soaring Perpendicular and Flamboyant churches; Renaissance architects in Florence revived classical forms (Brunelleschi's dome). Moscow's Kremlin cathedrals blended Byzantine and Italian styles.
cultures/culture-late-medieval/panels/3/: Giotto's naturalism transformed Western art; the Renaissance and Flemish painting depicted sacred scenes with new realism. In Russia Andrei Rublev's Trinity icon (c. 1411) became the classic image of Orthodox spirituality.
cultures/culture-late-medieval/panels/4/: The Black Death decimated monasteries, but observant reform movements and the Devotio Moderna renewed religious life. Sergius of Radonezh inspired hundreds of Russian monasteries, Athonite hesychasm spread to the Slavs, and Ethiopian monastic movements of Ewostatewos and Takla Haymanot flourished.
cultures/culture-late-medieval/panels/5/: Feasts of the Passion and the dead
Devotion to the Passion, the Holy Name and the Five Wounds grew; All Souls and requiem Masses multiplied after plague. Ethiopia observed both Saturday and Sunday Sabbaths after 1450.
cultures/culture-late-medieval/panels/6/: Catherine of Siena advised popes, Bridget of Sweden founded an order, Julian of Norwich wrote Revelations of Divine Love and Margery Kempe dictated the first English autobiography. Joan of Arc was burned in 1431 and later canonised; witch-hunting treatises (Malleus Maleficarum, 1486) targeted women.
cultures/culture-late-medieval/panels/7/: Italian humanists revived classical and patristic learning; Greek scholars fleeing Byzantium taught Greek in Italy. Printing (c. 1450) multiplied Bibles and devotional books; new universities spread to Prague, Kraków and Uppsala.
cultures/culture-late-medieval/panels/8/: Portuguese voyages brought Catholicism to Kongo (1491), and Columbus' voyage (1492) began the Christianisation of the Americas under royal patronage. In China and Central Asia, Christianity vanished after the Mongol collapse.
cultures/culture-late-medieval/panels/9/: Lollards and Hussites were burned as heretics; crusades failed against Bohemia. Timur's campaigns devastated Christians across Persia, Mesopotamia and Central Asia, reducing the Church of the East to a remnant.
cultures/culture-late-medieval/panels/10: Jews were blamed for the Black Death and massacred; Spain expelled its Jews in 1492 and Portugal forcibly converted them in 1497. The Inquisition investigated conversos suspected of secret Judaism.
cultures/culture-late-medieval/panels/11: The Ottomans conquered the Balkans and Constantinople (1453), ruling Orthodox Christians through the millet system. Granada fell to Castile in 1492. In Egypt, Coptic Christians declined sharply under Mamluk pressure, and Christian Nubia ended.
cultures/culture-late-medieval/panels/12: The Avignon papacy and Western Schism led to councils claiming authority over popes; kings negotiated concordats controlling their churches. Moscow's autocephaly (1448) and the 'Third Rome' idea fused Orthodoxy with Russian rule.
